Hi — thanks for sending the redline. I reviewed the attachment briefly; we've flagged a couple of items internally that will need alignment before we can sign. Quick answers up front:

- Service provider vs. operator language: we can accept a 'service provider' classification for typical model inference and telemetry, but we cannot agree to language that treats Redwood as a data controller or allows unconstrained onward transfers.
- Onshore fallback: we can commit to an onshore fallback process for 'regulated telemetry' when specifically scoped in the addendum, subject to capacity and notice windows (proposal below).
- Subprocessor notice: we provide 30 days' notice of new subprocessors and a short objection window; for emergency vendors we will provide notice as soon as practicable and include compensating safeguards.

Proposed excerpt (replace Section 3.1 and 5.2):

"Service Provider; Limitations on Use. Provider is a service provider under applicable US state privacy laws, including CPRA/CPPA. Provider will process personal information solely on Customer's documented instructions and will not (a) sell, share, or retain personal information beyond the service relationship, or (b) use personal information to independently develop or train models for third-party use. Provider may use aggregated, de-identified telemetry for service improvement provided reasonable safeguards are applied and such data cannot be re-identified.

Onshore fallback. For Customer-designated regulated telemetry, Provider will: (i) route processing to onshore infrastructure upon 30 days' notice where capacity permits; (ii) provide a documented fallback runbook and estimated failover time; (iii) provide quarterly attestations that onshore fallback tests were performed. Where immediate onshore routing is required for emergency security incidents, Provider will initiate an expedited onboarding of fallback capacity and provide a post-incident report.

Subprocessors and objection rights. Provider will notify Customer of new subprocessors at least 30 days before onboarding, together with a summary of location and purpose. Customer may object within 14 days on reasonable security or legal grounds; parties will engage in good-faith remediation. For critical security or compliance subprocessors, Provider will provide a remedial plan or offer alternate architecture options."

Notes: two pragmatic points — (1) 'aggregated, de-identified telemetry' needs a clear definition in exhibit if BrightCare insists; (2) we should avoid a strict SLA guaranteeing onshore routing within X hours unless they accept reserved capacity pricing. Priyom, can you confirm whether a 30-day notice + quarterly attestation is operationally feasible?

Thanks Logan and Kim — this is helpful. BrightCare is generally comfortable with the service provider framing, and the onshore fallback language addresses our procurement team's primary concern as long as we have a testable runbook and quarterly attestations. A few clarifying points:

- Can Redwood add a short exhibit that defines "regulated telemetry" (examples: device-level diagnostics containing device identifiers, usage logs linked to patient identifiers)?
